```

How we are supposed to run kube-proxy in non-privileged mode with this setting preserved?

---

@khenidak According to my testing kube-proxy was running fine with `NET_ADMIN` and `SYS_RESOURCE` (except the sysctls).

I see your point now. kube-proxy is released as a single binary, you can't assume kube-proxy is containerized, despite most people use it that way. I don't know if you can remove these sysctls without making breaking changes.

Also, kube-proxy is one particular implementation of Services, but there can be others, you don't have to use kube-proxy, some people is working on a evolution on [kpng project](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kpng) , they should have this feedback to not carry over this past mistakes

nodes.title: kube-proxy: Optionally do privileged configs only
nodes.body:
A new `--init-only` flag is added that makes `kube-proxy` perform configuration that requires privileged mode and exit. It is intended to be executed in a privileged `initContainer`, while the main container may run with a stricter securityContext

#### What type of PR is this?

/kind feature
/sig network
/area kube-proxy

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Users don't like containers running with `privileged: true`. This PR allows the configs that _requires_ `privileged: true` to run in an `initContainer`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #112171

Well, it solves the problem, but nothing documented (yet)

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

Tested with an `initContainer` similar to
```yaml
initContainers:
  - name: kube-proxy-init
    command:
    - /usr/local/bin/kube-proxy
    - --config=/var/lib/kube-proxy/config.conf
    - --init-only
    image: registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:local
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    securityContext:
      privileged: true
    volumeMounts:
    - mountPath: /var/lib/kube-proxy
      name: kube-proxy
```
And the main kube-proxy container runs with:
```yaml
        securityContext:
          capabilities:
            add: ["NET_ADMIN", "SYS_RESOURCE"]
```

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?


```release-note
Added a new `--init-only` command line flag to `kube-proxy`. Setting the flag makes `kube-proxy` perform its initial configuration that requires privileged mode, and then exit. The `--init-only` mode is intended to be executed in a privileged init container, so that the main container may run with a stricter `securityContext`.
```

title: High cpu usage in json.compact call
body:
### What happened?

I was debugging performance of case with heavy watch traffic of CRD objects and found interesting suboptimality: we burn significant amount of CPU on json.compact calls that deserialize JSONs to validate correctness of already serialized objects: 
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2559168/169510517-e5b23c43-b15c-4f6d-adf1-cf36ccf6e203.png)

It looks like while in WatchServer.ServeHTTP we manage to reuse serialized objects (cachingObject) in object serialization: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7af5a7bfc51d0455d8b2322ae9e72ed66fb1b8f9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/watch.go#L247-L251, we then wrap this objects in metav1.Event object and serialize it again: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7af5a7bfc51d0455d8b2322ae9e72ed66fb1b8f9/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/endpoints/handlers/watch.go#L271

While that object consists of single enum and already serialized raw object it is expected that its serialization will be cheap. And it is for protobufs where we simply copy bytes:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7af5a7bfc51d0455d8b2322ae9e72ed66fb1b8f9/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/generated.pb.go#L187-L192

But for json, it's much more expensive:
* We return already serialized object if re.Raw is set (it is on watch code path): https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/7af5a7bfc51d0455d8b2322ae9e72ed66fb1b8f9/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/extension.go#L37-L51
* but golang's json serializer compacts that json to check its validity: https://github.com/golang/go/blob/d8762b2f4532cc2e5ec539670b88bbc469a13938/src/encoding/json/encode.go#L498

This validation happens in each watcher separately contributing to significant CPU usage.

### What did you expect to happen?

We won't deserialize/compact objects in each watch client separately.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Open watch for objects using json encoder
2. See pprofs.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

Hi, is it okay for me to try implement the cache solution if I'm totally new to the codebase?
Hey,  can I take a stab on it? if no one is working on it?

@mborsz @wojtek-t @shyamjvs poke ... anything we can do here for 1.26?

@akankshakumari393 looks like no one is working on this yet. so go for it.

Yes, I'm not aware of anyone working on this.

I'm afraid there is no trivial fix. The options I see:
* caching encoded metav1.WatchEvent inside of *cachingObject to allow reusing it for all watchers
   * the problem is that it requires some very specific handling of *cachingObjects in *WatchService.ServeHTTP which increases complexity of the code.
* making the serialization of metav1.WatchEvent cheaper, e.g. by somehow avoiding json.compact, e.g. by:
   * changing to other json serialization library (potentially quite large change)
   * changing golang's json serializer to drop the expensive json.compact validation of the MarshalJSON() result (this requires much more context on why it is needed), potentially conditionally.
     * @mknyszek, are you able to help us with understanding why this is needed/contacting us with someone from golang who can be able to help here?
* Some ugly hacks

Any other options?

I think that `json.compact` goes beyond a validity check. If I understand the code correctly, it's main purpose is to append JSON produced by a `MarshalJSON` method to a buffer, while simultaneously checking its validity (so you get an error if the `MarshalJSON` method produced something invalid) and compacting it (producing compact JSON is I believe the common case?). I think it may also escape characters but I didn't look too closely. Specifically, it's for situations like this: https://go.dev/play/p/U2j27dhAogr.

I'm not totally sure this can be avoided in general. It could do less, like just append the JSON it gets, but you lose some positives like better error checking and more consistent output (by compacting it).

Perhaps I'm misunderstanding the code though; I'm not too familiar on this codebase. Maybe @dsnet knows more?

Without looking into it further, this seems may be a similar problem as kubernetes/kube-openapi#315, but in the marshal direction, rather than unmarshal.

If you have benchmark to run, I can look into deeper later.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/113326 adds benchmark for this issue.

/cc

If we don't find a volunteer to tackle this in the next 2 weeks, I'll be happy to give it a try.
/assign

While thinking about the alternatives that @mborsz linked - @mknyszek, are you able elaborate a bit more about the problem you linked in the Go Playground snippet, specifically about the errors that additional validations in `compact` can uncover?

In our case the output is already compacted, hence attempting to compact it second time doesn't make sense. If we had, purely theoretically, an additional interface w/ a method named e.g. `MarshalAlreadyCompactedJSON` then we'd get rid of the problem altogether here, hence the question about other reasons for running the validations in `json.compact`.

Sure thing. AFAICT, the JSON encoding package needs to handle potentially arbitrary inputs from a `MarshalJSON` method call which may not be valid or compacted. I think any alternative interface would have to be "unsafe" in some sense as it might break internal `encoding/json` invariants (or if those invariants could be avoided, that probably needs a bigger restructuring of the package, which I know @dsnet was looking into at some point).

> Changing Go to solve the CRD watchers-related problem here would be pretty time-consuming, however. I'll probably try writing some POC with the solution @mborsz proposed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110146#issuecomment-1289296713 related to caching metav1.WatchEvent inside the cachingObject.

I think that having some quick POC for this option would help making a decision. I think it shouldn't be that complicated on top of what we already have, but I may be missing something. Seeing how invasive the changes are would help here - I don't think we will make reasonable decision without knowing that.

I took a quick look at it (can't comment on the branch, but here are my few comments)
- adding `GetCachedEvent` seems acceptable to me - I think there is a question about the exact interface it should have, but at the high-enough level it seems reasonable to me
- I need to double check, but I think outer encoder determines the embedded one - so maybe we could actually simplify stuff a bit; otoh, thanks to your current approach we're reusing most of existing logic/code which seems to be highly beneficial

So overall, the above approach makes a lot of sense to me.

I think the next steps are:
- clearing this branch a bit, so that it compiles and can be run (without yet adjusting/adding appropriate unit tests)
- running tests to assess the impact of this change
- getting a feedback from someone else from sig-apimachinery

Thanks Wojtek for early feedback.

@tosi3k will help with cleaning the code and making it reviewable.

json.compact hogging memory is a symptom of json encoding hogging memory.

I have no idea if the go team will accept it, but I'm working on a change which should fix it in the std library: https://go-review.git.corp.google.com/c/go/+/455776

After the refactoring that I did before, I have a PR that seems to generally address the problem describe here in a pretty clean way:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/120300


It still requires extending test cases, but it generally seems to be working as desired.

title: kubectl cp fails with absolute path on Windows
body:
### What happened?

I tried to copy a file from a running pod to my local machine using `kubectl cp` on Windows. I used the `$HOME` env var in Powershell and it failed to copy saying essentially no local path was specified.

```console
PS C:\> kubectl cp -n namespace -c container pod-0:/usr/lib/os-release C:\Temp\os-release.log
error: one of src or dest must be a local file specification
PS C:\> kubectl cp -n namespace -c container pod-0:/usr/lib/os-release $HOME\os-release.log
error: one of src or dest must be a local file specification
```

Using relative paths works. Also removing the `C:` allows the command to work:

```console
PS C:\> kubectl cp -n namespace -c container pod-0:/usr/lib/os-release \Temp\os-release.log
tar: Removing leading `/' from member names

PS C:\> cat C:\Temp\os-release.log

VERSION_CODENAME=focal
UBUNTU_CODENAME=focal

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected `kubectl cp` to succeed and copy the file to my local machine using `$HOME` or absolute paths like `C:\Users\me`

2. Copy any file from the container to any absolute path on Windows : `kubectl cp -n namespace -c container pod:/etc/os-release C:\Temp\os-release`

This applies to Windows environment variables as well, such as `$HOME`. Removing `C:` from the absolute path while in the `C:` drive in powershell **does** work. It seems like the `C:` is causing issues (my guess is that `kubectl` thinks `C` is a pod).

title: creationTimestamp: null is invalid since it isn't a string
body:
### What happened?

There seems to be a discrepancy between the Kubernetes openapi spec and the Go package with the `creationTimestamp`

### What did you expect to happen?

CRDs generated by `controller-gen` which uses `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` to be valid according to the Kubernetes openapi spec.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```console
# wget https://github.com/fluxcd/source-controller/releases/download/v0.22.5/source-controller.crds.yaml
# kubeconform -schema-location default -schema-location "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/yannh/kubernetes-json-schema/master/master/customresourcedefinition.json" source-controller.crds.yaml
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition gitrepositories.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition buckets.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition helmrepositories.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
source-controller.crds.yaml - CustomResourceDefinition helmcharts.source.toolkit.fluxcd.io is invalid: For field metadata.creationTimestamp: Invalid type. Expected: string, given: null
```

### Anything else we need to know?

At first I raised an issue at https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/issues/2623 since they seemed to be the culprit.
But received a response that they use `controller-gen` to generate the CRDs. So I looked into [controller-gen](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-tools) and they also do not set the `creationTimestamp` they import `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` for the generation of the metadata (where the creationTimestamp is part of)([source](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-tools/blob/8cb5ce83c3cca425a4de0af3d2578e31a3cd6a48/pkg/crd/spec.go#L26)).

So now the issue, in the package documentation ([link](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1#ObjectMeta)) of `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` it says the following about the `creationTimestamp`
```golang
// CreationTimestamp is a timestamp representing the server time when this object was
// created. It is not guaranteed to be set in happens-before order across separate operations.
// Clients may not set this value. It is represented in RFC3339 form and is in UTC.
//
// Populated by the system.
// Read-only.
// Null for lists.
// More info: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#metadata
// +optional
Creation[Time](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1#Time)stamp Time `json:"creationTimestamp,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,8,opt,name=creationTimestamp"`
```

So there is something in the docblock about Null for lists(?) but in the openapi spec of Kubernetes is this `Time` resource marked as string:
```json
"io.k8s.apimachinery.pkg.apis.meta.v1.Time": {
      "description": "Time is a wrapper around time.Time which supports correct marshaling to YAML and JSON.  Wrappers are provided for many of the factory methods that the time package offers.",
      "format": "date-time",
      "type": "string"
},
```
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/master/api/openapi-spec/swagger.json

So now, what is wrong here? Is it indeed allowed to be a string or null and should the openapi spec be an enum? Or is there something in`k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` wrong? Or should `controller-gen` explictly set the creationTimestamp to an string? 
The last one seems kinda wrong to me since it seems to me that the `k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1` should return data valid to the api spec.

I am sorry for all the text and if I did not understand something correctly :)
I don't develop in golang (or at all really) and the relation between the package and the openapi spec is quite vague for me.

I opened the issue here since it seems an issue affecting multiple things within the kubernetes namespace (golang package, openapi spec in this repo).

### Kubernetes version

<details>
kubectl version
Client Version: version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"23", GitVersion:"v1.23.5", GitCommit:"c285e781331a3785a7f436042c65c5641ce8a9e9", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2022-03-16T15:51:05Z", GoVersion:"go1.17.8", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"darwin/arm64"}

/cc @jpbetz @sttts 
/triage accepted
Hi I am new to K8s. Would like to try this issue out.  Any hints ?

@prakharporwal I think there needs to be a decision or discussion from one of the maintainers how this is supposed to work before there could be looked at a fix.

Appreciate the enthusiasm though ❤️

@jpbetz @sttts Sorry for the ping but could one of you chime in, which one of the proposed solutions is the way forward?

The current state of an official package generating invalid YAML according the the spec seems something that needs to be solved :)

And again a little nudge @jpbetz @sttts 

The current discrepancy breaks linters like [yannh/kubeconform](https://github.com/yannh/kubeconform) since they generate their ruleset based on the API spec.
The current state makes a generated CRD from an official package invalid according to rules based on the API spec.
Would be great if this can be fixed, so that we don't have to remove lines with `creationTimestamp: null` manually for our CI linting.

~`creationTimestamp` is an optional field in openAPIv3 and may be absent from the JSON but should never be set to `null`.~

~The go struct contains `json:",omitempty"` to direction serializers to omit the field from JSON if the go struct is null.~

~Would someone provide more more details on how the resources were serialized such that they contain `creationTimestamp: null`?~

edit: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3e26e104bdf9d0dc3c4046d6350b93557c67f3f4/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/time.go#L144 will set the field value to null, so for backward compatibility the correct fix here it probably to add `nullable: true` to the openAPIv3 schema for Time.

see https://gist.github.com/jpbetz/5a27c20b4f29d8ee1144af8f43e57a0b for the exact behavior.
cc @jiahuif @apelisse

From @liggitt, there is a bunch of backstory here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/67610, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/53464, https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/issues/68, https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/issues/119, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/104857

@apelisse pointed out to me a couple issues here that make this less practical to fix on the k8s side:

- Even if we add `nullable: true` in OpenAPIv3, it will only help in toolchains that are correctly consuming openapiv3, which is often not the case, and I'm not clear if it is the case in this specific issue.
- While `creationTimestamp` is one of the most obvious examples of a field that is allowed to be set to `null` but is not marked as nullable, the Kubernetes marshalling code allows for `null` in many cases, none of which are explicitly marked as `nullable: true`. For example, IIRC, in CRDs, all non-required fields may be set to null, and we don't require CRD authors to explicitly add `nullable: true` to the schemas.

Would it be possible for kubeconform to be modified to uniformly allow `null` for all non-required fields?

Also, code that uses the [applyconfigurations](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/applyconfigurations/doc.go) instead of the go structs will not produce null fields like this. It might be sufficient to use applyconfigurations for this case to avoid the immediate problem.

> While creationTimestamp is one of the most obvious examples of a field that is allowed to be set to null but is not marked as nullable, the Kubernetes marshalling code allows for null in many cases, none of which are explicitly marked as nullable: true. For example, IIRC, in CRDs, all non-required fields may be set to null, and we don't require CRD authors to explicitly add nullable: true to the schemas.

I'm not sure I agree the list of all types needing annotation is innumerable. My interpretation is that `nullable` controls whether `null` is ignored/omitted for during both serialization and deserialization, respectively. 

Go's JSON deserializer implicitly treats all null values as unset (in line with `nullable: false`). This applies to both native types and CRDs: 

> The JSON null value unmarshals into an interface, map, pointer, or slice by setting that Go value to nil. Because null is often used in JSON to mean “not present,” unmarshaling a JSON null into any other Go type has no effect on the value and produces no error. [source][(https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json](https://pkg.go.dev/encoding/json#Unmarshal))

There is only one exception to this: native types with custom `UnmarshalJSON` that directly handle `null` to override the default behavior. 

> To unmarshal JSON into a value implementing the Unmarshaler interface, Unmarshal calls that value's UnmarshalJSON method, including when the input is a JSON null. 

The (likely) exhaustive list of native types that I've found that implement custom JSON marshaling to handle null are:

(found using regex `\) (Unm|M)arshalJSON((?!func).|\n)*null`)

1. [runtime.RawExtension](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/03b434c9d447d3e78f91f130420c5a83e11c81b4/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/extension.go#L1-L51)
    used as a value
1. [runtime.Unknown](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9f9e7177a328ae47bac6b823d57a99dfbfd310b/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/embedded.go#L73-L95) (doesnt roundtrip for null/"" case. likely bug?)
    used only as pointer
1. [meta.v1.Time](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9f9e7177a328ae47bac6b823d57a99dfbfd310b/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/time.go#L98-L152)
    used as both a pointer and a value
1. [meta.v1.MicroTime](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f9f9e7177a328ae47bac6b823d57a99dfbfd310b/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/micro_time.go#L110-L161)
    used as both a pointer and a value
1. [meta.v1.FieldsV1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c5a8015bbae1e1095813d8e0719f017477dc7112/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/apis/meta/v1/helpers.go#L279-L295)
    only used as a pointer
1. [apiextensions.v1.JSON](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/694698ca3801fe5aa258d58c1e27ac7f88c29d35/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/v1/marshal.go#L123-L136)
    used both as pointer and value. 
1. [apiextensions.v1.JSONSchemaPropsOrStringArray](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/694698ca3801fe5aa258d58c1e27ac7f88c29d35/staging/src/k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver/pkg/apis/apiextensions/v1/marshal.go#L62-L92)
    only used as a pointer
1. [resource.Quantity](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c5a8015bbae1e1095813d8e0719f017477dc7112/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L650-L702)
    used both as pointer and value. Unmarshals `null` but does not marshal `null`

We need to apply the `nullable` annotation in the schema only to all places where `null` does not mean `unset` - where `null` is an interpreted value. This is especially important if our types possibly marshal into `null`.

To avoid cases where pointer usages are marked nullable, I think we also need to ensure the code generator only  insert `nullable: true` into the non-pointer usages of types with a `+k8s-openapi:nullable` marker, and not the pointer-based ones.

> Go's JSON deserializer implicitly treats all null values as unset. This applies to both native types and CRDs:

That's true for native types, but it's not correct for custom resources. Go's JSON deserializer will unmarshal `{"foo":null}` to `map[string]interface{}{"foo":null}`. https://go.dev/play/p/u4nxaMn-iqo

We do a specific post-process step to drop explicitly null fields which were not marked as nullable in the schema (see `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults`). Setting `nullable` in the schema will *break* this pruning step and will preserve explicit `null` values.

> This applies to both native types and CRDs:
> That's true for native types, but it's not correct for custom resources. 

My mistake. The property that non-nullable null => unset for CRDs is not given by the the JSON deserializer. But the overall argument still holds. `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` is what gives the property to CRDs that `nullable: false` implies `null = unset` in k8s schemas. JSON deserializer for native types.

> Setting nullable in the schema will break this pruning step and will preserve explicit null values.

I'm not sure I would see this as broken for the cases I've proposed. I am proposing to add  `nullable` only to value-typed usages of the listed types which  marshal their empty value into explicit null values. 

`PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` would not prune fields like `creationTimestamp` as we've specified in OpenAPI since they also have a default set (kube-openapi code generator forces all structs to have `{}` default).

```json
          "creationTimestamp": {
            "allOf": [
              {
                "$ref": "#/components/schemas/io.k8s.apimachinery.pkg.apis.meta.v1.Time"
              }
            ],
            "default": {},
            "description": "..."
          },
```

I see two alternatives for fixing schema to be able to validate JSON that these types marshal into:

1. Permit the null by adding nullable annotation
2. Ignore the null by removing implicit `{}` default applied to struct types that marshal their empty values into `null`. Clients should know to also apply `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` as we do to both native types and CRDs.

Both options are consistent and work for my purposes (kubectl-validate & Declarative Validation). The second carries the risk of not representing the reality in apiserver if `null` possibly could unmarshal into anything other than empty, but I dont think that applies to any of our current concrete cases.

> `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` would not prune fields like `creationTimestamp` as we've specified in OpenAPI since they also have a default set (kube-openapi code generator forces all structs to have `{}` default).

wow... that default is completely invalid for metav1.Time, which serializes as a string... first we need to stop setting defaults of an invalid type in the openapi

> I see two alternatives for fixing schema to be able to validate JSON that these types marshal into:
> 
> 1. Permit the null by adding nullable annotation

I don't think we should add `nullable` for fields which the server doesn't return null for, like creationTimestamp.

> 2. Ignore the null by removing implicit `{}` default applied to struct types that marshal their empty values into `null`. Clients should know to also apply `PruneNonNullableNullsWithoutDefaults` as we do to both native types and CRDs.

Knowing that both built-in types and custom resource types will drop null for property fields (or unmarshal to empty), this seems like the best option among several not-great ones.

> The second carries the risk of not representing the reality in apiserver if null possibly could unmarshal into anything other than empty, but I dont think that applies to any of our current concrete cases.

A custom unmarshaler turning null into a not-empty case would be bizarre... there's already problems with nulls in some patch types (like json merge patch) explicitly meaning "drop this value", so we already try to steer people away from nullable fields, and a `null` meaning something other than `empty` would be problematic already.

Seems `"creationTimestamp":null` still exists.

I reuse the podTemplateSpec in my CRDs, when patching the CRD object, it reports `metadata.creationTimestamp: field not declared in schema"`. Log the creationTimestamp, it has a null value, `"metadata":{"creationTimestamp":null,`. 

My kubernetes version is 1.30.0, I use the k8s client to create the CRD objects.

title: CRI getFsInfo logs errors for valid filesystems mounted after kubelet start
body:
**What happened**:

New overlay filesystems created for Pods after kubelet start trigger repeated error messages. For example:

```
cri_stats_provider.go:375] Failed to get the info of the filesystem with mountpoint "/var/lib/containers/storage/overlay/2243263dc8ba6c55d8867d3e47bcaaa145d15f0ace19420824d639d86defe2e3/merged": failed to get device for dir "/var/lib/containers/storage/overlay/2243263dc8ba6c55d8867d3e47bcaaa145d15f0ace19420824d639d86defe2e3/merged": could not find device with major: 0, minor: 83 in cached partitions map.
```

Error messages are logged every 10 seconds for every filesystem created after kubelet start. For large kubelet nodes, this issue creates an excessive amount of error logs.

**What you expected to happen**:

New overlay filesystems created for Pods after kubelet start should not log error messages.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

Use cri_stats_provider with cri-o and configure overlay storage. UsingLegacyCadvisorStats() needs to return false per https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/pull/3054 for cri_stats_provider to be used. Start with an empty /var/lib/containers/storage and schedule Pods on the node.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

As part of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/59475, cadvisor.GetFsInfoByFsUUID() was changed to cadvisor.GetDirFsInfo() in getFsInfo(); however, the test for cadvisorfs.ErrNoSuchDevice was not modified, changing how getFsInfo() handles a cache miss from cadvisor. 

cadvisor caches UUIDs/partitions/mounts on kubelet start and the cache is never refreshed. Given that it's expected that getFsInfo() will fail to retrieve data from cadvisor (see comments in ImageFsStats() and https://github.com/kubernetes/heapster/issues/1793), this condition should not be logged as an error. Alternatively, cadvisor fs could be modified to refresh on cache miss enabling getFsInfo() to return data on these filesystems.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.18.6
- CRI: CRI-O

title: Containers with "m" used as abbreviation in memory limits fail to start on Linux, and consume 1e+9 too much memory on Windows
body:
## Background

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-compute-resources-container/

  Limits and requests for memory are measured in bytes. You can express memory as a plain integer or as a fixed-point integer using one of these suffixes: E, P, T, G, M, K. You can also use the power-of-two equivalents: Ei, Pi, Ti, Gi, Mi, Ki. For example, the following represent roughly the same value:

  `128974848, 129e6, 129M, 123Mi`

## Bug

If someone uses a lowercase letter, for example `m`, that has inconsistent behavior between Windows & Linux. `m` is a valid suffix for CPU but not memory.

> Note: `docker` command line options do support `m`, `b`, `k` and `g`. [docker resource constraints](https://docs.docker.com/config/containers/resource_constraints/#limit-a-containers-access-to-memory)

On Linux, the `m` prefix is dropped if it's included as part of a memory resource. This resource allocation will create an allocation of 300 bytes, not 300 Megabytes or Mebibytes. That's too small and container startup will fail. See [full error logs](#full-error-logs) below.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx-test1
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: library/nginx
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 800m
    ports:
      - containerPort: 80
  nodeSelector:
    "beta.kubernetes.io/os": linux
```



On Windows, the `m` prefix is treated the same as `M`. This resource allocation will be 300 Megabytes, and container startup will succeed.

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: iis-test2
spec:
  containers:
  - name: iis
    image: mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore/iis:windowsservercore-ltsc2019
    resources:
      limits:
        cpu: 1
        memory: 800m
    ports:
      - containerPort: 80
  nodeSelector:
    "beta.kubernetes.io/os": windows
```

This would have the same effect on resources as `docker run --memory 800m -d mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore/iis:windowsservercore-ltsc2019` on Windows.


## Proposed Fixes

There are a few different places this could be fixed. They're not mutually exclusive, so I'm asking SIG-Node and API reviewers to consider the impact of each.

Parsing cpu & memory limits separately is not feasible as the same string parser is shared for all resource types.

### Fix 1 - reject memory limits below a certain threshold in the admission controller

This would be the most consistent as the failure would happen immediately, and be consistent on both Windows & Linux. Let's start with a strawman proposal of 10Mi as the container minimum. Windows actually needs more like 200Mi, but I think 10Mi would be enough to catch the most egregious mistakes such as "10m".

Source Locations: 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f47da8a75d13590322a4e1df502cf6629b2c36fa/plugin/pkg/admission/limitranger/admission.go#L213



### Fix 2 - reject memory limits with `m` in kubelet

This would fail later, but won't involve changes to the apiserver, common APIs or admission controller. The error messages can still be made consistent between Linux & Windows, but different minimums can be enforced in each side. This could be implemented in the code that creates the container configs before passing them to CRI.

Source locations:

See previous discussion in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/49442

Tightening pod API validation is not generally feasible, since that can cause existing persisted data to be treated as invalid, and in some cases, not be able to be updated in order to be deleted. See https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/64841

If the windows CRI cannot allocate sub-megabyte memory values, I would expect an attempt to do so to either get as close as possible (e.g. 1MB) or error.

Just to clarify here - the bad impact is actually on Linux, not Windows. Windows assumes a "m" in a memory unit is Mi. Linux drops ignores the letter. That means `800m` = 800 bytes on Linux, but 800 Mi on Windows

"800m" actually means 800 *millibytes*, which isn't sensible. The config is very wrong and apparently there's another bug somewhere, too. Is kubelet not using the resource.Quantity type to interpret this value before handing it to the container runtime?

> the bad impact is actually on Linux, not Windows

both can be bad. linux fails to run the container (as expected for an untenably small memory amount), when what we would have preferred is for the API to validate some minimum sane memory size was specified. windows allows a container to consume orders of magnitude more memory than was reserved in resourcequota for it, right?
https://github.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/blob/master/pkg/api/resource/quantity.go#L46
Do the platforms both behave the same if you pass the intended value of "800M" or "800Mi"? (capital M)
yes, both work with `M` or `Mi`. Windows works with `m`, but Linux doesn't.

Are you sure it's turned into 800 bytes on linux? I'd expect this to be rounded to either 1 byte or 0 bytes if it's handled correctly.

800m should not work on windows, either, unless windows can allocate 6.4 bits to a program? :)
I do think that validation should forbid memory requests smaller than a byte, but as Jordan points out, the validation change is dangerous.

I think it rounds to the nearest byte, and below a certain threshold (like 4MB), containers will just not start

> I do think that validation should forbid memory requests smaller than a byte, but as Jordan points out, the validation change is dangerous.

I think it can be done relatively safely with ratcheting validation. memory requests that are fractions of a byte are certainly a mistake, and do not work properly on any container runtime.

I think it would be best if windows also interpreted 'm' values as a request for 0 bytes and failed them, rather than "helping" people and training them to do the wrong thing :/
If these always fail, then the risk of breaking an existing setup is pretty low and it might be safe to forbid them in the API.

> If these always fail, then the risk of breaking an existing setup is pretty low and it might be safe to forbid them in the API.

that was my claim in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/64841#issuecomment-405436597. I'm happy to resurrect the ratcheting for the truly impossible-to-succeed cases.

even more than that, the current handling makes ResourceQuota ineffective for memory on windows

I'm not sure where the `m` is being interpreted at the moment. need more digging. That was a valid abbreviation in the Moby/Docker codebase which Windows is still using [doc](https://docs.docker.com/config/containers/resource_constraints/#limit-a-containers-access-to-memory)
